title: Centering prayer
hookLine: a quiet method from Trappist monks in the 1970s, rooted in older teaching

lines: A SIMPLE FORM FOR BUSY PEOPLE.
cards: Massachusetts, the early 1970s. Young people are knocking at a Trappist monastery, and some of them are on their way to Eastern teachers of meditation. The monks notice.
Some of those young people were raised Catholic, and say they never heard that their own Church had a tradition of silent prayer.
The abbot asks a question: could we put that old tradition into a simple form, something a busy person could actually do? Three monks, the abbot among them, get to work.

teach.b: The monastery was Saint Joseph's Abbey in Spencer, Massachusetts. The abbot was Thomas Keating, and with him were William Meninger and Basil Pennington. They called it centering prayer.
First, the roots. They didn't invent the silence.

They drew on the desert fathers, on an old English book you'll meet tomorrow, and on Jesus's words in the Sermon on the Mount, in the Douay-Rheims: "But thou when thou shalt pray, enter into thy chamber, and having shut the door, pray to thy Father in secret."
The inner room. Second, the method.

You choose a sacred word, short and simple: God, Jesus, Abba, peace, love. It isn't a mantra repeated over and over; it's a sign of your intention. You sit comfortably, eyes closed, and introduce the word gently.
That's it. Third, the thoughts. They will come: plans, worries, the grocery list.
When you notice you're caught up in one, return, ever so gently, to the sacred word.
In this method, every return counts as a small yes. Fourth, what it's for. Not a special experience.

Not emptying the mind. Its founders describe it as consenting to God's presence and action within, trusting that something is happening even when it feels like nothing. Catholics don't all agree about it.
Some parishes and retreat houses teach it; some Catholic writers are more cautious, and prefer prayer with more words and images. Both sit inside the Church.

how: People who practice centering prayer usually sit for about twenty minutes, often twice a day, using a chosen sacred word as a sign of consent to God, and some join small groups that sit together in parishes and retreat houses.

o: a prayer said facing the center of the church
a technique for emptying the mind of every thought
silent prayer with one sacred word, as consent to God

games.q: what's inside the method — tap the pairs.

s: centering prayer means emptying your mind
thoughts will come; the method is to return gently to the sacred word, as consent to God.
the sacred word is repeated nonstop, like a chant
it's introduced gently, as a sign of intention, and returned to when you notice you've drifted.
its founders drew on older Christian teaching
the desert fathers, the Cloud of Unknowing and Jesus's words about praying in the inner room.

games.q: you're sitting in silent prayer and you notice you've spent the last minute planning dinner. what does centering prayer say to do?
o: stop and start the whole prayer over.
return gently to your sacred word.
games.why: just return, ever so gently. the founders treat every return as a small yes, not a failure.

practice: Pick one short word: if you pray, God, or Jesus, or Abba; if you don't, peace, or yes. Close your eyes, let the word arrive once, softly, as a sign you're willing to be here, then let it go.
When you notice you're thinking, don't scold yourself; just come back to the word, gently.

wordCard.voice: Centering prayer. A simple method of silent prayer from Trappist monks in the 1970s: one sacred word, and a gentle return, as consent to God's presence. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: an inner storeroom, the chamber Jesus names in Matthew 6:6, which centering prayer's founders pointed to.

carryVoice: Your line: consent to his presence. A mind that wanders comes home like a dog called back, not scolded. Day two hundred forty-four, done.
